exercises.title: Say hello
exercises.prompt:
Write a function `greet(name)` that returns the string
`Hello, <name>!` - so `greet("Ada")` returns `Hello, Ada!`.

Return the string. Do not print it. Returning and printing are
different things, and almost everything you write from here on
returns.
hints: An f-string is the shortest route: f"Hello, {name}!"
`return` hands a value back to the caller; `print` only writes to the screen.
exercises.solution:
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

exercises.title: Celsius to Fahrenheit
exercises.prompt:
Write `to_fahrenheit(celsius)` returning the temperature in
Fahrenheit. The formula is `F = C x 9/5 + 32`.

Return a float. 100 degrees Celsius is 212.0 Fahrenheit.
hints: Use `9 / 5`, not `9 // 5`. Integer division would throw away the fraction.
exercises.solution:
def to_fahrenheit(celsius):
    return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32

exercises.title: Split seconds into h:m:s
exercises.prompt:
Write `hms(total_seconds)` that turns a whole number of seconds into a
tuple `(hours, minutes, seconds)`.

`hms(3661)` is `(1, 1, 1)`. Every part must be a whole number.

tests.name: one hour one minute one second
all parts are ints
tests.code: assert all(isinstance(p, int) for p in hms(3661))

hints: `//` divides and throws away the remainder; `%` keeps only the remainder.
divmod(a, b) gives you both at once.
exercises.solution:
def hms(total_seconds):
    minutes, seconds = divmod(total_seconds, 60)
    hours, minutes = divmod(minutes, 60)
    return hours, minutes, seconds

exercises.title: Initials
exercises.prompt:
Write `initials(full_name)` returning the uppercase initials of every
word, separated by dots and ending with one.

`initials("ada lovelace")` returns `"A.L."`.
Extra spaces between words must not produce empty initials.
hints: `text.split()` with no argument splits on any run of whitespace and drops empties.
Build the pieces in a list, then `''.join(...)` them.
exercises.solution:
def initials(full_name):
    return "".join(word[0].upper() + "." for word in full_name.split())

exercises.title: Format a price
exercises.prompt:
Write `price(amount)` returning the amount as a string with a leading
dollar sign, a thousands separator and exactly two decimals.

`price(1234.5)` returns `"$1,234.50"`.
hints: Format specs compose: f"{amount:,.2f}" adds separators and fixes the decimals.
exercises.solution:
def price(amount):
    return f"${amount:,.2f}"

exercises.title: Letter grade
exercises.prompt:
Write `grade(score)` mapping a 0-100 score to a letter:
90 and above `A`, 80-89 `B`, 70-79 `C`, 60-69 `D`, below 60 `F`.

A score outside 0-100 must raise `ValueError`.

tests.name: rejects over 100
rejects negative

hints: Check the invalid range first and raise, then the happy path reads top to bottom.
Order your comparisons from highest to lowest so each `elif` only needs one bound.

exercises.title: Leap years
exercises.prompt:
Write `is_leap(year)` returning True for leap years in the Gregorian
calendar.

A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except centuries, which
must also be divisible by 400. 1900 was not a leap year. 2000 was.
hints: The whole rule fits in one boolean expression.
Write it as: divisible by 4 AND (not divisible by 100 OR divisible by 400).
exercises.solution:
def is_leap(year):
    return year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0)

exercises.title: Sum up to n
exercises.prompt:
Write `sum_to(n)` returning the sum of every whole number from 1 to `n`
inclusive. `sum_to(5)` is 15. `sum_to(0)` is 0.

Write the loop yourself this time, even though a formula exists.
hints: `range(1, n + 1)` stops *before* the second argument, so add one.
Start an accumulator at 0 before the loop, not inside it.

exercises.title: FizzBuzz as a list
exercises.prompt:
Write `fizzbuzz(n)` returning a list of length `n`. For each position
from 1 to n: multiples of 15 become `"FizzBuzz"`, multiples of 3 become
`"Fizz"`, multiples of 5 become `"Buzz"`, everything else is the number
itself as an `int`.
hints: Test for 15 first. If you test 3 first, no number ever reaches the FizzBuzz branch.

exercises.title: Second largest
exercises.prompt:
Write `second_largest(numbers)` returning the second largest *distinct*
value in the list.

`[5, 1, 5, 3]` gives 3, because both fives are the same value.
If there is no second distinct value, return `None`.
hints: `set(numbers)` removes duplicates in one step.
Sort the distinct values, then index from the end - but check the length first.

exercises.title: Squares of the even numbers
exercises.prompt:
Write `even_squares(numbers)` returning a list containing the square of
every even number in the input, in the original order.

Use a single list comprehension.
hints: The shape is [expression for item in iterable if condition].
exercises.solution:
def even_squares(numbers):
    return [n * n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]

exercises.title: Middle three characters
exercises.prompt:
Write `middle_three(text)` returning the three characters in the middle
of an odd-length string of length 3 or more.

`middle_three("abcde")` returns `"bcd"`.
Anything shorter than 3, or of even length, returns `""`.
hints: The middle index is len(text) // 2.
Slice from middle - 1 up to middle + 2.

exercises.title: Tidy up a name
exercises.prompt:
Write `tidy(name)` that strips leading and trailing whitespace,
collapses any internal run of whitespace to one space, and
title-cases the result.

`tidy("  ada   LOVELACE ")` returns `"Ada Lovelace"`.
hints: split() then ' '.join() collapses whitespace in one move.
str.title() capitalises each word.
exercises.solution:
def tidy(name):
    return " ".join(name.split()).title()

exercises.title: Acronym
exercises.prompt:
Write `acronym(phrase)` returning the uppercase first letter of each
word joined together, with no separators.

`acronym("portable network graphics")` returns `"PNG"`.
exercises.solution:
def acronym(phrase):
    return "".join(word[0].upper() for word in phrase.split())

exercises.title: Count the words
exercises.prompt:
Write `word_count(text)` returning a dict mapping each lowercase word to
how many times it appears. Split on whitespace and ignore case.

`word_count("a A b")` returns `{"a": 2, "b": 1}`.
hints: dict.get(key, 0) gives you a default instead of a KeyError.
collections.Counter does this in one line - try it after you have written the loop.

exercises.title: Look up without crashing

tests.name: no get used
tests.code: import inspect; assert '.get(' not in inspect.getsource(lookup)

hints: `in` tests for a key, not a value.
Beware of `if data[key]:` - that would treat 0 and '' as missing.

exercises.title: Unique, order preserved
exercises.prompt:
Write `unique(items)` returning a list with duplicates removed, keeping
the first occurrence of each value in its original position.

`unique([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])` returns `[3, 1, 2]`.
A plain `set()` would lose the order, so you need both structures.
hints: Track what you have already emitted in a set, and append to a list.
Membership testing in a set is constant time; in a list it is not.

exercises.title: Sort people by surname
exercises.prompt:
Write `by_surname(names)` sorting a list of `"First Last"` strings by
last name, then by first name. Return a new list; do not modify the
input.

tests.name: sorts by last name
tests.code: assert by_surname(['Ada Lovelace', 'Grace Hopper']) == ['Grace Hopper', 'Ada Lovelace']

tests.name: ties break on first name
tests.code: assert by_surname(['Bob Smith', 'Alice Smith']) == ['Alice Smith', 'Bob Smith']

tests.name: input untouched
tests.code:
src = ['B X', 'A X']
by_surname(src)
assert src == ['B X', 'A X']

hints: sorted() returns a new list; list.sort() changes the original.
A key function returning a tuple sorts by the first element, then the second.

exercises.title: Top N by value
exercises.prompt:
Write `top_n(scores, n)` where `scores` is a dict mapping names to
numbers. Return a list of the `n` names with the highest scores,
highest first. Break ties alphabetically by name.
hints: Sort by a tuple key: negative score first, then the name.
Slicing past the end of a list is safe - it just gives you what is there.

exercises.title: Positions of a value
exercises.prompt:
Write `positions(items, target)` returning a list of every index where
`target` appears. Use `enumerate` rather than counting by hand.
exercises.solution:
def positions(items, target):
    return [i for i, item in enumerate(items) if item == target]

exercises.title: Pair two lists up
exercises.prompt:
Write `pair_up(names, scores)` returning a dict built from two parallel
lists. If one list is longer, ignore the extra entries.
hints: zip stops at the shorter of its inputs, which is exactly what you want here.
dict() accepts an iterable of pairs.
exercises.solution:
def pair_up(names, scores):
    return dict(zip(names, scores))

exercises.title: Total by category
exercises.prompt:
Given a list of dicts like
`{"category": "food", "amount": 12.5}`, write `totals(rows)` returning a
dict mapping each category to the sum of its amounts.
hints: Reach for dict.get(key, 0) again, or collections.defaultdict(float).

exercises.title: The mutable default trap
exercises.prompt:
This function is broken. Every call shares the same list, so results
leak between calls:

    def add_item(item, basket=[]):
        basket.append(item)
        return basket

Fix `add_item` so that calling it with no basket always starts a fresh
one, while still allowing a caller to pass their own list in.

tests.name: accepts a caller's list
tests.code:
mine = ['x']
assert add_item('y', mine) == ['x', 'y']
assert mine == ['x', 'y']

tests.name: no mutable default
tests.code:
import inspect
sig = inspect.signature(add_item)
assert sig.parameters['basket'].default is None

hints: Default arguments are evaluated once, when the function is defined.
Use None as a sentinel and build the real default inside the body.

exercises.title: Flexible arguments
exercises.prompt:
Write `describe(*values, **options)` returning a string of the form
`"3 values | sep=- upper=True"`.

The count comes first, then a pipe with spaces around it, then each
keyword option as `key=value`, sorted by key and separated by single
spaces. With no options, return just `"3 values"`.

tests.name: with options
tests.code: assert describe(1, 2, 3, sep='-', upper=True) == '3 values | sep=- upper=True'

tests.name: options are sorted
tests.code: assert describe(1, b=2, a=1) == '1 values | a=1 b=2'

exercises.title: Factorial
exercises.prompt:
Write `factorial(n)` recursively. `factorial(0)` is 1.
Raise `ValueError` for negative input.

tests.name: rejects negatives

hints: Write the base case first, then the recursive step.
Without a base case you get a RecursionError, not a wrong answer.

exercises.title: Divide without crashing
exercises.prompt:
Write `safe_div(a, b)` returning `a / b`, or `None` when `b` is zero.
Catch the exception rather than testing for zero first, so you see how
`try` reads.
hints: Catch ZeroDivisionError specifically. A bare `except:` would swallow real bugs.

exercises.title: Validate before you trust
exercises.prompt:
Write `validate_age(value)` returning the age as an `int`.

Raise `TypeError` if the value is not a string or a number.
Raise `ValueError` if it cannot be read as a whole number, or is
outside 0 to 130.

tests.name: rejects nonsense
rejects out of range
rejects wrong type

hints: int('old') raises ValueError; int([1]) raises TypeError.
Check the type first, then the conversion, then the range.

exercises.title: Parse the numbers you can
exercises.prompt:
Write `parse_ints(values)` returning a list of the entries that convert
cleanly to `int`, skipping the ones that do not.

`parse_ints(["1", "x", "3"])` returns `[1, 3]`.
hints: Put the try inside the loop, around only the one line that can fail.
None raises TypeError, not ValueError - catch both.

exercises.title: Count the non-empty lines
exercises.prompt:
A file named `notes.txt` already exists in the working directory.
Write `count_lines(path)` returning how many lines in it contain
something other than whitespace.
hints: `with open(path) as fh:` closes the file even if something raises.
A line of only spaces is not empty until you strip it.
exercises.setup:
LINES = ["first", "", "  ", "second", "third"]
with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    fh.write(chr(10).join(LINES) + chr(10))

exercises.title: Round-trip through JSON
exercises.prompt:
Write `save(path, data)` and `load(path)` that write a dict to a file as
JSON and read it back. The value that comes back must equal the value
that went in.

tests.name: round trips
writes valid json

hints: json.dump writes to a file object; json.dumps returns a string.
Always pass encoding='utf-8' so the code behaves the same on every platform.

exercises.title: Days between two dates
exercises.prompt:
Write `days_between(a, b)` taking two `YYYY-MM-DD` strings and returning
the whole number of days between them. The result is never negative.
hints: date.fromisoformat parses the string for you.
Subtracting two dates gives a timedelta; .days is the whole-day part.

exercises.title: Most common letter
exercises.prompt:
Write `most_common_letter(text)` returning the letter that appears most
often, ignoring case and anything that is not a letter.

Ties are broken alphabetically. An input with no letters returns `None`.
hints: str.isalpha() tells you whether a character is a letter.
Counter.most_common does not break ties for you - sort by (-count, letter).

exercises.title: any and all
exercises.prompt:
Write two functions:

`all_positive(numbers)` - True when every number is greater than zero.
An empty list counts as True.

`has_negative(numbers)` - True when at least one number is below zero.
hints: all() and any() short-circuit, so they stop at the first decisive value.

exercises.title: Palindrome check
exercises.prompt:
Write `is_palindrome(text)` ignoring case, spaces and punctuation.

`"A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"` is a palindrome.

tests.name: classic
tests.code: assert is_palindrome('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama') is True

hints: Build a cleaned string of only alphanumeric characters, lowercased.
text[::-1] reverses a string.

exercises.title: Invert a mapping
exercises.prompt:
Write `invert(mapping)` returning a new dict with keys and values
swapped. If two keys share a value, the last one seen wins.
hints: A dict comprehension reads {value: key for key, value in mapping.items()}.
exercises.solution:
def invert(mapping):
    return {value: key for key, value in mapping.items()}

exercises.title: Running totals
exercises.prompt:
Write `running_total(numbers)` returning a list where each position
holds the sum of everything up to and including it.

`[1, 2, 3]` becomes `[1, 3, 6]`.
hints: Keep one accumulator outside the loop and append after each update.
itertools.accumulate does this too - compare once yours works.
exercises.solution:
def running_total(numbers):
    out = []
    total = 0
    for number in numbers:
        total += number
        out.append(total)
    return out

exercises.title: Write an iterator by hand
exercises.prompt:
Build a class `Countdown(n)` that iterates from `n` down to 1.

Implement `__iter__` and `__next__` yourself. Do not use a generator -
the point is to see what a generator is doing underneath.

tests.name: works in a for loop
tests.code:
seen = []
for v in Countdown(2):
    seen.append(v)
assert seen == [2, 1]

tests.name: raises StopIteration

hints: __iter__ returns the thing that has __next__ - often self.
__next__ raises StopIteration when there is nothing left.

exercises.title: Fibonacci, lazily
exercises.prompt:
Write a generator function `fib()` yielding the Fibonacci sequence
starting 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 and never ending.

Because it is lazy, an endless generator costs nothing until you take
values from it.

tests.name: each call is independent
tests.code:
a, b = fib(), fib()
assert next(a) == next(b) == 0

hints: A function containing `yield` returns a generator when called.
Track two values and swap them: a, b = b, a + b.

exercises.title: Flatten nested lists
exercises.prompt:
Write a generator `flatten(items)` yielding every non-list value from an
arbitrarily nested list, left to right.

`flatten([1, [2, [3, 4]], 5])` yields 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
Use `yield from` for the recursive step.
hints: `yield from sub` forwards every value the inner generator produces.
Check isinstance(item, list), not Iterable, or strings will unravel.

exercises.title: Count the calls
exercises.prompt:
Write a decorator `counted` that adds a `calls` attribute to the
wrapped function, counting how many times it has run. The wrapped
function must keep its own name and docstring.

tests.name: counts
passes arguments through
keeps the name

hints: functools.wraps copies __name__, __doc__ and friends onto the wrapper.
Attach the counter to the wrapper, then return the wrapper.

exercises.title: A decorator that takes arguments

tests.name: passes arguments

hints: Three nested functions: the factory, the decorator, then the wrapper.
The factory takes the argument; the decorator takes the function.

exercises.title: A context manager class
exercises.prompt:
Write a class `Tag(name)` used as a context manager that appends
`"<name>"` to a list when it enters and `"</name>"` when it leaves.

The list must be reachable as `tag.parts`. The closing tag must still be
written if the block raises, and the exception must still propagate.

tests.name: wraps the block
tests.code: t = Tag('b') with t: t.parts.append('hi') assert t.parts == ['', 'hi', '']

tests.name: closes on error
tests.code: t = Tag('i') try: with t: raise RuntimeError('boom') except RuntimeError: pass assert t.parts == ['', '']

tests.name: does not swallow the error

hints: __exit__ runs whether or not the block raised.
Returning a truthy value from __exit__ suppresses the exception - do not.

exercises.title: contextlib version
exercises.prompt:
Write `temporarily(mapping, key, value)` - a context manager built with
`@contextlib.contextmanager` that sets `mapping[key] = value` on entry
and restores the previous state on exit, including the case where the
key did not exist before.

tests.name: sets and restores
tests.code:
d = {'a': 1}
with temporarily(d, 'a', 99):
    assert d['a'] == 99
assert d['a'] == 1

tests.name: removes a key that was absent
tests.code:
d = {}
with temporarily(d, 'new', 5):
    assert d['new'] == 5
assert 'new' not in d

tests.name: restores after an error

hints: Everything before `yield` is the enter step; everything after is exit.
Wrap the yield in try/finally so cleanup survives an exception.

exercises.title: A vector type
exercises.prompt:
Write a class `Vector(x, y)` supporting:

* `v1 + v2` and `v1 - v2`
* `v * 3` (scaling by a number)
* `v1 == v2` by value
* `repr(v)` returning `Vector(1, 2)`
* `abs(v)` returning the length
hints: __eq__ should return NotImplemented for unrelated types, not False.
__repr__ is for developers; make it look like the call that builds the object.

exercises.title: A sequence of your own
exercises.prompt:
Write `Deck()` holding the strings `"A"` through `"E"`. Support
`len(deck)`, `deck[0]`, negative indexing, iteration and `"C" in deck`
by implementing only `__len__` and `__getitem__`.
hints: Delegating to the underlying list gives you slicing for free.
Python builds iteration and `in` out of __getitem__ when __iter__ is absent.

exercises.title: Validate on assignment
exercises.prompt:
Write `Temperature` with a `celsius` property that rejects anything
below absolute zero (-273.15) with `ValueError`, and a read-only
`fahrenheit` property computed from it.

tests.name: rejects impossible values
rejects on later assignment
fahrenheit is read only

hints: The setter stores to a differently named attribute, usually _celsius.
Assigning in __init__ goes through the setter, so validation happens there too.

exercises.title: Alternative constructors
exercises.prompt:
Write `Event` with `year`, `month` and `day`, plus a classmethod
`from_string("2026-01-31")` that builds one, and a staticmethod
`is_valid_string(text)` returning whether a string has that shape.
hints: A classmethod receives the class, so `cls(...)` also works for subclasses.
A staticmethod is a plain function that happens to live on the class.

exercises.title: Less boilerplate
exercises.prompt:
Rewrite a point type as a frozen, ordered dataclass `Point(x, y)`.

It must be immutable, comparable, sortable and usable as a dict key.

tests.name: immutable

hints: @dataclass(frozen=True, order=True) gives you all of it.
frozen=True is what makes instances hashable.

exercises.title: Abstract base classes
exercises.prompt:
Define an abstract base `Shape` with an abstract `area()` and a
concrete `describe()` returning `"<ClassName> with area <area>"`.

Then write `Rectangle(w, h)` and `Circle(r)`. Instantiating `Shape`
directly must raise `TypeError`.
exercises.starter:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
import math


class Shape(ABC):
    pass

tests.name: abstract cannot be built

hints: type(self).__name__ gives the real subclass name at runtime.
A class with an unimplemented @abstractmethod cannot be instantiated.

exercises.title: Chunk an iterable
exercises.prompt:
Write `chunks(iterable, size)` yielding lists of at most `size` items.
It must work on a generator, not only a list, and must not read the
whole input into memory first.

tests.name: works on a generator
tests.code: assert list(chunks((n for n in range(5)), 2)) == [[0, 1], [2, 3], [4]]

tests.name: lazy
tests.code:
import itertools
inf = itertools.count()
assert next(iter(chunks(inf, 3))) == [0, 1, 2]

tests.name: rejects a size of zero

hints: iter() on the input first, then islice repeatedly from that one iterator.
islice on a fresh iter() each time would restart from the beginning.

exercises.title: Memoise an expensive function
exercises.prompt:
Write `slow_fib(n)` computed by naive recursion, then make it fast with
caching. It must answer `slow_fib(35)` effectively instantly, and
expose a `cache_info()` from the standard library.

tests.name: fast enough to be cached
tests.code:
import time
start = time.monotonic()
slow_fib(35)
assert time.monotonic() - start < 1.0

hints: functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None), or functools.cache on 3.9 and later.
The decorator caches by arguments, so the recursion hits the cache too.

exercises.title: Type hints that mean something
exercises.prompt:
Annotate `first_or_default` fully: it takes a list of strings and an
optional default string, and returns a string.

The body is written for you. Add the annotations so that
`typing.get_type_hints` reports them.
exercises.starter:
def first_or_default(items, default="none"):
    return items[0] if items else default

tests.name: items is annotated
tests.code:
import typing
hints = typing.get_type_hints(first_or_default)
assert 'items' in hints

hints: list[str] works directly on modern Python; no typing import needed for it.
exercises.solution:
def first_or_default(items: list[str], default: str = "none") -> str:
    return items[0] if items else default

exercises.title: Balanced brackets
exercises.prompt:
Write `balanced(text)` returning True when every `(`, `[` and `{` is
closed in the right order. Ignore any other character.
hints: A stack is just a list with append and pop.
On a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its partner.

exercises.title: A ring buffer
exercises.prompt:
Write `RingBuffer(capacity)` that keeps only the most recent `capacity`
items. Support `push(item)`, `items()` returning oldest to newest, and
`len()`.

tests.name: keeps recent items
tests.code:
b = RingBuffer(3)
for n in [1, 2, 3, 4]:
    b.push(n)
assert b.items() == [2, 3, 4]

tests.name: length is capped
tests.code:
b = RingBuffer(2)
for n in range(10):
    b.push(n)
assert len(b) == 2

hints: collections.deque(maxlen=n) drops from the far end automatically.

exercises.title: Build and reverse a linked list
exercises.prompt:
Write `Node(value, next=None)`, `to_list(head)` turning a chain into a
Python list, `from_list(values)` building a chain, and `reverse(head)`
returning the new head of the reversed chain.

Reverse it iteratively, in place, without building a Python list first.

tests.name: empty chain
tests.code: assert to_list(reverse(from_list([]))) is not None or True

tests.name: no list used in reverse
tests.code:
import inspect
src = inspect.getsource(reverse)
assert 'to_list' not in src and 'from_list' not in src

hints: Reversal needs three names: previous, current and the saved next.
Save current.next before you overwrite it, or you lose the rest of the chain.

exercises.title: Write a hash map
exercises.prompt:
Implement `HashMap(buckets=8)` with `put(key, value)`, `get(key,
default=None)` and `__len__`, using a list of buckets and Python's
`hash()`. Handle collisions with chaining, and overwrite on a repeat
key.

tests.name: overwrites
tests.code:
m = HashMap()
m.put('a', 1)
m.put('a', 2)
assert m.get('a') == 2 and len(m) == 1

tests.name: survives collisions
tests.code:
m = HashMap(buckets=1)
for i in range(20):
    m.put(i, i * 2)
assert m.get(19) == 38 and len(m) == 20

tests.name: counts entries

exercises.prompt:

`target`. The naive version is O(n^2) and is too slow for the last

exercises.solution:
from collections import Counter


def count_pairs(numbers, target):
    seen = Counter()
    total = 0
    for value in numbers:
        total += seen[target - value]
        seen[value] += 1
    return total

exercises.solution:
import logging


def make_logger(name, stream):
    logger = logging.getLogger(name)
    logger.handlers.clear()
    logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
    logger.propagate = False
    handler = logging.StreamHandler(stream)
    handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(levelname)s:%(message)s"))
    logger.addHandler(handler)
    return logger

hints: Check the balance first, then do both updates, then commit.
On failure call conn.rollback() so no half-finished write survives.
exercises.solution:
def transfer_copies(conn, from_title, to_title, amount):
    try:
        row = conn.execute(
            "SELECT copies FROM books WHERE title = ?",
            (from_title,)).fetchone()
        if row is None or row[0] < amount:
            raise ValueError("not enough copies")
        conn.execute(
            "UPDATE books SET copies = copies - ? WHERE title = ?",
            (amount, from_title))
        conn.execute(
            "UPDATE books SET copies = copies + ? WHERE title = ?",
            (amount, to_title))
        conn.commit()
    except Exception:
        conn.rollback()
        raise

exercises.solution:
import asyncio


async def fetch_limited(urls, limit):
    gate = asyncio.Semaphore(limit)

    async def one(url):
        async with gate:
            return await fetch(url)

    return list(await asyncio.gather(*(one(u) for u in urls)))
exercises.setup:
import asyncio

STATE = {"live": 0, "peak": 0}


async def fetch(url):
    STATE["live"] += 1
    STATE["peak"] = max(STATE["peak"], STATE["live"])
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return f"got {url}"
    finally:
        STATE["live"] -= 1

exercises.title: Refuse to escape the root
exercises.prompt:
Write `safe_join(root, user_path)` returning the resolved path inside
`root`, or raising `ValueError` when the user path escapes it.

`"../../etc/passwd"` and an absolute path must both be rejected.

tests.name: normal file
tests.code:
from pathlib import Path
assert safe_join('data', 'a/b.txt') == (Path('data').resolve() / 'a' / 'b.txt')

tests.name: rejects traversal
rejects an absolute path
rejects a sneaky middle traversal

hints: Resolve both paths first, then test containment - string prefixes lie.
Path.is_relative_to does the containment check for you.
exercises.solution:
from pathlib import Path


def safe_join(root, user_path):
    base = Path(root).resolve()
    candidate = (base / user_path).resolve()
    if not candidate.is_relative_to(base):
        raise ValueError("path escapes the root directory")
    return candidate

exercises.title: Softmax without overflow
exercises.prompt:
Write `softmax(scores)` turning a list of numbers into probabilities
that sum to 1.

Subtract the maximum before exponentiating, or large inputs overflow.

tests.name: order is preserved
tests.code:
p = softmax([1, 3, 2])
assert p[1] > p[2] > p[0]

hints: exp(1000) overflows a float; exp(1000 - 1001) does not.
Subtracting a constant from every score leaves the result unchanged.
exercises.solution:
import math


def softmax(scores):
    if not scores:
        return []
    top = max(scores)
    exps = [math.exp(s - top) for s in scores]
    total = sum(exps)
    return [e / total for e in exps]

exercises.title: Split the data honestly
exercises.prompt:
Write `train_test_split(rows, test_ratio, seed)` returning
`(train, test)`.

The split must be reproducible for a given seed, must not lose or
duplicate any row, and must not mutate the input.

tests.name: sizes
tests.code:
train, test = train_test_split(list(range(100)), 0.2, 1)
assert len(test) == 20 and len(train) == 80

tests.name: nothing lost
tests.code:
train, test = train_test_split(list(range(50)), 0.3, 7)
assert sorted(train + test) == list(range(50))

tests.name: reproducible
tests.code:
a = train_test_split(list(range(30)), 0.25, 42)
b = train_test_split(list(range(30)), 0.25, 42)
assert a == b

tests.name: different seeds differ
tests.code:
a = train_test_split(list(range(60)), 0.25, 1)
b = train_test_split(list(range(60)), 0.25, 2)
assert a != b

tests.name: input untouched
tests.code:
src = list(range(10))
train_test_split(src, 0.5, 1)
assert src == list(range(10))

hints: random.Random(seed) gives a private generator, so you do not disturb global state.
Shuffle a copy, then slice.
exercises.solution:
import random


def train_test_split(rows, test_ratio, seed):
    shuffled = list(rows)
    random.Random(seed).shuffle(shuffled)
    cut = int(len(shuffled) * test_ratio)
    return shuffled[cut:], shuffled[:cut]
